analysis.one_liner: Expands health coverage by banning preexisting-condition denials, extending Medicaid, and subsidizing premiums through private insurers.
analysis.headline: The health care overhaul became law on March 23, 2010, after the Senate passed it 60–39 and the House adopted the Senate version 219–212, with no Republican votes and 34 Democrats opposed in the final House count.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill requires nearly all Americans to carry health insurance, bans insurers from denying people for preexisting conditions or capping lifetime benefits, and extends Medicaid to the lowest-income families. It pays for new coverage with subsidies funneled through private insurance companies, annual fees on insurers and drug and device makers, slower Medicare payment growth, and higher taxes on high earners. It also delivered industry wins, including 12 years of protection for brand-name biologic drugs from cheaper copies.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured Americans, people with preexisting conditions, young adults who can stay on a parent's plan until 26, low-income families who gain Medicaid, and middle-income families who get premium tax credits and reduced out-of-pocket costs up to 400% of the poverty line [S4]. Small employers with up to 25 lower-wage workers get a health coverage tax credit of up to 50% [S4]. Medicare beneficiaries get brand-drug discounts in the coverage gap and a free annual wellness visit [S4]. Health insurers also gain: the mandate plus subsidies steer tens of millions of new customers into private plans, and no public alternative survived the process [S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured and people with preexisting conditions

how_it_helps.text: Bans insurers from denying or dropping coverage for preexisting conditions and limits how much premiums can vary by anything other than age, tobacco use, family size, or location [S4].
Prohibits lifetime and annual dollar limits on benefits, so a serious illness can no longer exhaust a policy's cap [S4].

Extends Medicaid starting in 2014 to people with incomes up to 133% of the federal poverty line, with the federal government paying 100% of the cost of covering newly eligible people in 2014–2016 [S4].
Gives refundable premium tax credits and reduced out-of-pocket limits to people earning between 100% and 400% of poverty who buy coverage through new state-run exchanges [S4].
Requires plans to cover recommended preventive services with no copays and lets young adults stay on a parent's plan until age 26 [S4].
Gives small employers with up to 25 employees a tax credit covering up to 50% of their workers' health coverage costs [S4].
Requires drug makers to discount brand-name drugs in the Medicare Part D coverage gap and adds a no-cost-sharing annual wellness visit to Medicare [S4].
Requires every hospital to publish its standard charges and requires insurers to report how premiums are spent and rebate customers when less than 80–85% goes to actual care [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the Medicaid expansion, premium subsidies, and public health programs [S4]. Individuals face a penalty for going without coverage starting in 2014, with exemptions for those who cannot afford it [S4]. High-income households pay a 0.9% Medicare surtax on wages over $200,000 ($250,000 for couples) and lose part of the medical expense deduction as its threshold rises to 10% [S5]. Insurers, brand drug makers, and device makers pay annual fees; employers with more than 50 full-time workers face fines for not offering coverage; flexible spending accounts are capped at $2,500; and a 40% excise tax hits the most expensive employer health plans [S4][S5].
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, high earners, and health industries

drawbacks.text: Starting in 2014, most Americans must carry health insurance or pay a penalty, with exemptions for those who cannot afford it, religious objectors, people not lawfully present, and the incarcerated [S4].
High-income households pay a 0.9% Medicare payroll tax increase on wages over $200,000 ($250,000 for couples), and a 40% excise tax applies to high-cost employer health plans [S5].
People with high medical costs lose ground: flexible spending account contributions are capped at $2,500 and the itemized medical expense deduction threshold rises from 7.5% to 10% of income [S5].

The bill cuts Medicare payment growth for hospitals, nursing homes, home health, and other providers, and reduces payments to hospitals that serve large numbers of uninsured patients once more people gain coverage — pressure that falls hardest on safety-net hospitals in poor communities [S5].
Brand-name biologic drugs get 12 years of protection before cheaper copies can be approved, delaying price competition on some of the most expensive medicines [S4].

All new subsidized coverage runs through private insurance companies — the public insurance option was deleted from the final bill — so federal dollars pay private premiums rather than fund a government-run plan [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers what its supporters promised — guaranteed coverage regardless of health status, an income-based system of help paying for it, and Medicaid for the poorest families — funded largely by fees on the health industry and taxes on high earners rather than by cuts to core Medicare benefits [S4][S5]. The trade-offs are real: nearly everyone must buy coverage or pay a penalty, safety-net hospitals lose payments as coverage expands, brand drug makers won a 12-year shield from cheaper copies, and every new subsidy dollar flows through private insurers because the public option was stripped out [S4][S5]. On balance the gains for ordinary people substantially outweigh the costs, but the design permanently locks in the industry it regulates.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed a small military tax bill unanimously, the Senate swapped its contents for the full health care overhaul and passed it 60–39, the House accepted the Senate version 219–212, and the President signed it into law.

narrative.text: Introduced on September 17, 2009 as the 'Service Members Home Ownership Tax Act' — a narrow bill extending the first-time homebuyer tax credit to military personnel serving abroad and raising partnership return penalties [S2].
The House passed that shell bill 416–0 on October 8, 2009 under a fast-track procedure requiring a two-thirds vote, before any health care language had been added to it [S9][S3].

The Senate then replaced the bill's contents with the full health care overhaul; on November 21, a 60–39 vote ended the debate on taking it up — all 58 Democrats plus two independents for, all 39 Republicans against [S10].

Senate Republicans made six attempts to send the bill back to the Finance Committee during December floor debate; each was rejected, by margins including 42–58, 41–57, 41–53, 42–57, and 45–54, and one was tabled 56–41 [S11][S12][S13][S14][S15][S16].
Cloture on the bill itself was invoked 60–39 on December 23, and the Senate passed the bill 60–39 on December 24, 2009, with identical party splits [S17][S18].
The House agreed to the Senate version 219–212 on March 21, 2010 — 219 Democrats in favor, zero Republicans, with 34 Democrats joining all 178 Republicans opposed [S19].
President Obama signed the bill on March 23, 2010, making it Public Law 111-148, the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act [S8][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Uninsured Americans and people with preexisting conditions gained guaranteed access to coverage, and health insurers came out ahead too, winning a steady stream of subsidized customers under new rules and fees that their rivals in a public plan would have avoided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The uninsured, and insurers who gained customers

sides.party_line_note: Senate cloture and passage split 60–39 along party lines — every Democrat and independent in favor, every Republican opposed — and the final House vote was 219–212, with all 219 yes votes from Democrats, no Republican yes votes, and 34 Democrats joining 178 Republicans against.

industries.note: The bill bans preexisting-condition denials, rescissions, and lifetime limits, requires insurers to rebate premiums when less than 80–85% goes to care, and imposes an annual fee on the industry [S4][S5]. But the individual mandate and premium subsidies steer tens of millions of paying customers into private plans, and the public option was deleted, making private insurers the permanent channel for federal coverage spending [S4].

The bill raises Medicaid drug rebates, requires brand-drug discounts in the Medicare coverage gap, and imposes an annual fee on branded drug sales [S4][S5]. In exchange it grants brand biologics 12 years of market protection before cheaper biosimilars can be approved [S4].

The bill slows Medicare payment growth, cuts Medicaid disproportionate-share payments as uninsurance falls, and requires hospitals to publish standard charges [S4][S5]. Hospitals offset this by treating far more paying, insured patients once coverage expands [S4].

Employers with more than 50 full-time workers face fines for failing to offer coverage or imposing waiting periods over 60 days; those with 200 or more must auto-enroll new employees; all must report coverage value on W-2s [S4][S5].
An annual fee applies to device manufacturers and importers with gross sales over $5 million beginning in 2011 [S5].
A 0.9% hospital insurance tax increase applies to wages above $200,000 for individuals and $250,000 for joint filers, funding the coverage expansion [S5].
A 10% excise tax is imposed on indoor tanning services starting July 1, 2010 [S5].
